findings.title: Pin and verify the build-time installer
findings.whyItBreaks: Each build downloads mutable content from the network and executes it as root with sh. Because neither an immutable version nor an integrity digest is specified, an upstream compromise or changed installer silently changes the built image and can execute arbitrary code.

findings.title: Pin and verify the downloaded installer
findings.whyItBreaks: Every rebuild downloads and executes whatever bytes this URL serves at that moment. A compromised or changed upstream endpoint can run arbitrary commands in the build and alter the produced image without any repository change or integrity verification.

findings.title: Pin and verify the installer before executing it
findings.whyItBreaks: Every image build downloads and executes whatever this URL (or a redirect target) returns as root. A compromised or changed upstream response, DNS/proxy manipulation, or a transient error page becomes arbitrary build-time code execution.

findings.title: Preserve missing-key errors in the exported helper
findings.whyItBreaks: Load returns ErrMissing for an absent key, but this exported API discards it and returns "". A caller cannot distinguish a missing key from a key intentionally stored with an empty string, so it can treat failed lookups as real data.

findings.title: Preserve missing-key errors from the exported loader
findings.whyItBreaks: Discarding ErrMissing makes a missing key indistinguishable from an existing key whose value is "". As an exported API, LoadOrDefault forces every caller to treat a lookup failure as legitimate data.

findings.title: Preserve missing-key errors in LoadOrDefault
findings.whyItBreaks: For an absent key, Load returns ErrMissing at line 10, but this helper discards it and returns "". That is indistinguishable from a present key whose stored value is legitimately empty, so callers cannot safely distinguish lookup failure from data.

findings.title: Wait for result sends before returning
findings.whyItBreaks: Each send now runs in an untracked goroutine, so Run returns immediately for non-empty jobs. A caller that closes results after Run returns will cause a send-on-closed-channel panic; callers also cannot rely on all results being available when Run completes, unlike the base implementation.

findings.title: Preserve result completion before Run returns
findings.whyItBreaks: Each send is now detached from Run, so Run may return before any result is delivered. A caller that closes or consumes results after Run returns—safe with the previous synchronous implementation—can either miss results or panic when a still-running producer sends on the closed channel.

findings.title: Wait for result sends before returning
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously, Run returned only after every result was sent. It now launches sends and immediately returns. A valid caller can close its caller-owned results channel after Run returns, causing these goroutines to panic with "send on closed channel"; callers also lose the completion guarantee without any replacement synchronization mechanism.

findings.title: Preserve the Log callback signature
findings.whyItBreaks: Changing func(string) to func(string, ...string) breaks consumers that pass or assign logger.Log as a func(string), causing an upgrade-time compile failure even though direct one-argument calls remain valid.

findings.title: Preserve Log's original function type
findings.whyItBreaks: In Go, func(string, ...string) is not assignable to func(string). Existing downstream code such as `var sink func(string) = logger.Log`, or callbacks that require func(string), will fail to compile after this upgrade even though direct one-argument calls still work.

findings.title: Require both admin status and tenant ownership
findings.whyItBreaks: Using || returns true for a non-admin whose tenant matches the record, and for an admin from a different tenant. Either session can delete a record that the prior authorization rule denied.

findings.title: Keep tenant matching for administrators
findings.whyItBreaks: With an admin session from tenant A and a record from tenant B, the new OR expression returns true. This bypasses the prior tenant-isolation check and allows cross-tenant record deletion.

findings.title: Require admin status before allowing record deletion
findings.whyItBreaks: A session with isAdmin=false and the same tenantId now receives true. This bypasses the prior admin-only deletion requirement and permits a non-admin tenant member to delete any record in that tenant.

findings.title: Propagate invalid-settings errors instead of returning defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: Malformed JSON or a missing/wrong-typed field previously threw to updateFontSize at line 20, preventing save. It now becomes { theme: "light", fontSize: 14 }, so updateFontSize overwrites the persisted theme while concealing the invalid source data.

findings.title: Preserve parse failures instead of saving default settings
findings.whyItBreaks: A partial payload such as `{ "theme": "dark" }` now becomes the default settings. `updateFontSize` then changes its font size and saves it, replacing the user's dark theme with `light`; previously validation threw before `save` ran. The exported parser also makes malformed input indistinguishable from a legitimate default configuration.

findings.title: Preserve parse failures before saving settings
findings.whyItBreaks: Invalid persisted input is now converted to defaults instead of failing. For example, `{ "theme": "dark", "fontSize": "bad" }` passed to updateFontSize becomes `{ "theme": "light", "fontSize": <new size> }` and is saved, silently replacing the user's valid dark-theme selection. Previously parseSettings threw and prevented save from running.

findings.whyItBreaks: The exported pageCount contract requires a page for a non-empty remainder. pageCount(1, 10) now returns 0, and pageCount(11, 10) returns 1, causing consumers to omit the final partial page.

findings.title: Query artifacts at the reported branch commit
findings.whyItBreaks: When the requested branch and "verified" resolve to different commits, the result reports builtFrom as the branch commit while returning artifacts from the verified commit. Consumers therefore receive an internally inconsistent build report.

findings.title: Use the selected commit for report artifacts
findings.whyItBreaks: When branch resolves to a different commit than "verified", builtFrom identifies the branch commit but artifacts are fetched from the verified commit. Consumers receive a self-contradictory BuildReport, and a build without a verified ref now fails despite the requested branch resolving successfully.

findings.title: Use the branch commit when loading report artifacts
findings.whyItBreaks: When ref(branch) differs from ref("verified"), the report declares builtFrom as the requested branch commit but returns artifacts belonging to the verified commit. Consumers therefore receive artifacts attributed to the wrong build.

findings.title: Apply the positive limit before returning entries
findings.whyItBreaks: For any positive limit smaller than all.length, recentEntries now returns every reversed entry rather than at most limit. Its existing caller passes 20; renderFeed then writes each returned entry, extending its nominal 20-slot output when there are more than 20 entries.

findings.title: Honor the requested result limit
findings.whyItBreaks: For every positive limit, the new return path returns all reversed entries rather than at most limit. renderFeed passes 20 at line 9; with more than 20 entries its loop writes past the initially sized array and returns more than 20 feed items.

findings.title: Restore the limit cap for positive limits
findings.whyItBreaks: For any positive limit smaller than all.length, this returns every reversed entry instead of at most limit. renderFeed passes 20 at line 9, so an input with 21 entries grows its initially 20-element output to 21 entries.

findings.title: Count only emitted entries in the manifest header
findings.whyItBreaks: With one live and one stale entry, the manifest declares `# entry-count: 2` but emits one data row. Consumers using the header to validate or read the manifest receive an internally inconsistent contract.

findings.title: Count only emitted manifest entries
findings.whyItBreaks: Stale entries are removed from rows, but line 22 still supplies entries.length to the # entry-count header. A manifest with one live and one stale entry declares entry-count: 2 while containing one entry.

findings.title: Count only emitted manifest entries
findings.whyItBreaks: Stale entries are removed from rows, but the header still reports entries.length. A manifest with stale entries therefore declares more entries than it contains, breaking consumers that use # entry-count to validate or parse the manifest.

findings.title: Retain the exported legacy formatter
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing exported `FormatLegacyID` is a source-incompatible API change: downstream packages that format existing legacy identifiers will no longer compile. The diff includes neither a replacement nor a version/migration boundary.

findings.title: Restore the exported legacy formatter
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing exported ids.FormatLegacyID makes any downstream consumer of the established legacy-ID API fail to compile after upgrading.

findings.title: Retain the exported legacy formatter
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing exported ids.FormatLegacyID makes downstream packages that use the supported legacy-ID API fail to compile after upgrading; there is no compatibility replacement.

findings.title: Preserve the shippingQuote export
findings.whyItBreaks: This module previously exported `shippingQuote`; it now exports only the differently named `quoteShipping` from another module. Existing consumers importing `shippingQuote` from `src/orders` will fail type-checking or have no such runtime export after upgrading.

findings.title: Keep the exported shippingQuote compatibility wrapper
findings.whyItBreaks: The base revision exported shippingQuote from src/orders.ts, but this revision exports only quoteShipping from a new module. Existing consumers importing shippingQuote from the established orders module will fail to compile on upgrade.

findings.title: Restore the shippingQuote compatibility export
findings.whyItBreaks: shippingQuote was an exported API in the base revision, but this change removes it and exports only quoteShipping from a new module. Existing consumers importing shippingQuote from src/orders will fail TypeScript compilation or ESM module linking after upgrade.

findings.title: Return unauthorized for malformed stored hashes
findings.whyItBreaks: token_hash() always returns str, but hmac.compare_digest raises TypeError when stored_hash is None or another incompatible type. Previously equality returned false, allowing guard() to return {"status": 401}; now the exception skips that failure-closed path and turns a missing/malformed stored credential into a server error.

findings.title: Return the transformed input instead of always throwing
findings.whyItBreaks: Every call to the public execute(input): string API now throws, so callers cannot receive the uppercase string that the implementation returned before this change.

findings.title: Restore execute's string result
findings.whyItBreaks: execute is exported with a string return contract, but every invocation now throws. Consumers cannot receive the transformed input and the public API is unusable for its prior behavior.

findings.title: Restore execute's string result
findings.whyItBreaks: execute previously returned the uppercased input, but this changed implementation unconditionally throws. Every consumer of the exported function now fails instead of receiving its declared string result.

findings.title: Keep viewers eligible for the read-only path
findings.whyItBreaks: An active viewer with fewer than five attempts now fails isEligible and handle returns "rejected" at line 24. This bypasses handle's explicit viewer behavior at line 25, which previously returned "read-only" for that same request.

findings.title: Keep active viewers on the read-only path
findings.whyItBreaks: An active viewer with fewer than five attempts now fails isEligible and handle returns "rejected", so it can no longer reach the retained viewer-specific "read-only" behavior at line 25.

findings.title: Preserve the viewer read-only path
findings.whyItBreaks: An active viewer below the attempt limit now fails isEligible and handle returns "rejected" at line 24. Previously it passed eligibility and returned "read-only" at line 25, which is now unreachable for every viewer.

findings.title: Do not require payment to save a draft
findings.whyItBreaks: For { state: "draft", payment: "missing" }, this changed predicate now returns false, so saveDraft returns "blocked" instead of "saved". A draft can legitimately be saved before payment is recorded.

findings.title: Keep draft saving independent of payment status
findings.whyItBreaks: For { state: "draft", payment: "missing" }, the new payment conjunct makes canProceed false. saveDraft shares this predicate and therefore returns "blocked", whereas it previously saved the draft. Payment may govern submission but should not prevent persisting an unpaid draft.

findings.title: Keep saving drafts independent of payment
findings.whyItBreaks: Adding payment === "paid" to canProceed makes saveDraft({ state: "draft", payment: "missing" }) return "blocked". An unpaid draft is the normal state that must remain saveable; payment legitimately governs submission, not draft persistence.

findings.title: Read files from the selected channel head
findings.whyItBreaks: For any channel whose head differs from stable, the returned Snapshot reports the requested channel's commit but contains files from stable. Consumers cannot reliably read or publish the revision identified by snapshot.commit.

findings.title: Read files from the published channel head
findings.whyItBreaks: The snapshot reports `commit` as the requested channel's head but populates `files` from `stable`. When those refs differ, consumers receive file contents that do not belong to the reported commit or channel.

findings.title: Read files from the published channel head
findings.whyItBreaks: For any channel whose head differs from "stable", the returned Snapshot.commit identifies that channel's head but Snapshot.files contains stable's files. Consumers will publish or inspect content that does not match the advertised commit and channel.

findings.title: Honor the limit argument
findings.whyItBreaks: The added `limit` parameter promises callers control over result count, but the function still hard-codes `max_count = 10`; for example, `build("x", 3)` returns ten entries rather than three.

findings.title: Honor the requested result limit
findings.whyItBreaks: `build(prefix, limit=10)` promises that the supplied limit controls the result count, but the body still unconditionally assigns `max_count = 10`. For example, `build("item", 3)` returns 10 entries rather than 3.

findings.title: Honor the new limit parameter
findings.whyItBreaks: `limit` promises to cap the result, but the implementation still always iterates `max_count = 10`; for example, `build("x", 3)` returns ten values. This public callable contract is unusable even though no in-repo callers currently exercise it.

findings.title: Reject non-positive values in parse_positive_int
findings.whyItBreaks: `parse_positive_int("-1")` returns `-1`, so its changed public contract is false; `charge("-1")` consequently returns `-100` instead of rejecting a non-positive amount.

findings.title: Reject non-positive values in parse_positive_int
findings.whyItBreaks: The new public name promises a positive integer, but int(value) accepts 0 and negatives. Consequently charge(-1) returns -100 cents, so callers relying on the renamed contract can create negative charges instead of receiving validation failure.

findings.title: Enforce positive values in parse_positive_int
findings.whyItBreaks: The renamed public function promises a positive integer, but int(value) returns 0 and negative integers unchanged. Callers can therefore receive values that violate the function's stated contract, including zero or negative charges through charge().

findings.title: Restore the defensive DataFrame copy
findings.whyItBreaks: Callers that retain df and use the returned transformed frame now find their original DataFrame's value column silently overwritten. The prior implementation explicitly copied df before applying the mapping, so this is an observable mutation-contract regression.

findings.title: Preserve the input DataFrame
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously the function updated a copy and left df unchanged. It now overwrites df directly, so callers that retain the source DataFrame for subsequent processing observe mapped values instead of the original data.

findings.title: Enforce positivity in parse_positive_int
findings.whyItBreaks: The public name promises a positive integer, but the unchanged body parses "-1" as -1 and defaults invalid input or "0" to 0. Its in-repo consumer therefore emits negative or zero charges (for example, "-1" becomes -100), and external callers cannot rely on the promised contract.

findings.title: Reject non-positive values in parse_positive_int
findings.whyItBreaks: `parse_positive_int` returns `-1` for `"-1"` and `0` for `"0"`, contradicting its public name. Its caller then computes `charge("-1")` as `-100` at line 7.

findings.title: Reject non-positive values in parse_positive_int
findings.whyItBreaks: The new name promises a positive integer, but the unchanged body parses and returns negative inputs unchanged. Consequently, charge("-2") calls this function and returns -200 rather than rejecting or treating the amount as invalid.

findings.title: Borrow `items` when debugging it
findings.whyItBreaks: `dbg!(items)` evaluates and consumes the `Vec<String>`; the subsequent `items.len()` then borrows a moved value, causing a Rust compile error.

findings.title: Borrow items when printing debug output
findings.whyItBreaks: `dbg!(items)` evaluates to and drops the owned `Vec<String>` in this standalone statement. The following `items.len()` therefore uses a moved value and produces Rust error E0382.

findings.title: Borrow items when logging
findings.whyItBreaks: `dbg!(items);` consumes the `Vec<String>`; the subsequent `items.len()` then borrows a moved value and fails with Rust error E0382.

findings.title: Compute paths from the revision advertised by the changeset
findings.whyItBreaks: When `pinnedTag` resolves to a revision different from `latest`, `fromRevision` remains the pinned revision but `changedPaths` are computed against `latest`. Consumers replaying these paths on `fromRevision`, as the exported Changeset contract specifies, receive a delta from the wrong baseline and can apply incorrect or missing changes.

findings.title: Compute paths from the advertised revision
findings.whyItBreaks: When pinnedTag resolves to a revision other than latest, changedPaths is computed from latest while fromRevision remains the pinned revision. This violates the Changeset contract that consumers replay paths on exactly fromRevision, producing a mismatched changeset.

findings.title: Compute paths from the declared replay revision
findings.whyItBreaks: When pinnedTag resolves differently from "latest", changedPaths is computed against latest while fromRevision remains the pinned revision. Consumers therefore replay a delta for one revision on top of another, which can omit required changes or apply incompatible paths.

findings.title: Update the query for the renamed email column
findings.whyItBreaks: After this migration renames users.email to users.contact_email, src/query.sql still executes SELECT email FROM users. On an upgraded database that query fails because email no longer exists.

findings.title: Update queries to use the renamed column
findings.whyItBreaks: After this migration, `users.email` no longer exists, but `src/query.sql:1` still executes `SELECT email FROM users`, which will fail with an unknown-column error.

findings.title: Update the query to use the renamed column
findings.whyItBreaks: After this migration, users.email no longer exists, but src/query.sql still executes SELECT email FROM users. Any execution after upgrade fails with a missing-column error.

findings.title: Restore environment-based billing credential loading
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported makeClient() no longer rejects missing configuration and instead embeds a bk_live credential in source. Every deployment ignores its BILLING_API_KEY, routes billing calls through this single exposed credential, and cannot rotate or isolate credentials through normal environment configuration.

findings.title: Restore environment-based billing credentials
findings.whyItBreaks: A billing credential is now embedded in source and silently used when BILLING_API_KEY is absent. The secret will be exposed to every repository reader and all deployments will operate under one shared account instead of their configured account.

findings.title: Remove the committed live billing credential
findings.whyItBreaks: A production-looking bk_live credential is now embedded in source, exposing it to every repository reader and forcing every deployment to use the same credential instead of its configured, independently rotatable key.

findings.title: Preserve failure for an unset billing key
findings.whyItBreaks: makeClient is exported and previously threw when BILLING_API_KEY was absent. It now returns a seemingly valid BillingClient using a fallback literal, so callers cannot distinguish missing configuration from successful client construction.

findings.whyItBreaks: `user.isAdmin === false` now bypasses this guard; for an archived project, execution reaches `db.delete(project.id)`, so any non-admin can permanently purge it. Conversely, administrators are always denied.

findings.title: Preserve the missing-settings fallback
findings.whyItBreaks: load_settings() returns None for a nonexistent path, and startup() now immediately indexes that value. Any startup with a missing settings file raises TypeError instead of returning the prior default worker count of 1.

findings.title: Restore defaults when the settings file is missing
findings.whyItBreaks: `load_settings()` returns `None` for a nonexistent path, so this now evaluates `None["workers"]` and raises `TypeError`. Before this change, the same supported missing-file path started with one worker.

findings.title: Restore fallback for an absent settings file
findings.whyItBreaks: load_settings returns None when path does not exist (line 7). With the fallback removed, startup evaluates None["workers"] and raises TypeError instead of preserving the previous default worker count.

findings.title: Propagate gateway submission failures
findings.whyItBreaks: When Gateway.Submit returns an error, Charge logs it and returns nil. Callers therefore cannot distinguish a declined or failed charge from a completed payment and may proceed with fulfillment or record the charge as successful.

findings.title: Propagate gateway submission failures
findings.whyItBreaks: When Gateway.Submit returns an error, Charge only logs it and then returns nil. Its exported API therefore makes a failed charge indistinguishable from a successful one, allowing callers to record or report a charge as completed.

findings.title: Propagate failed gateway submissions
findings.whyItBreaks: When Gateway.Submit returns an error, Charge logs it and returns nil. Its exported API now makes a failed charge indistinguishable from a successful one, so callers can continue as if payment completed.

findings.title: Keep the tenant ID in the settings cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: The cache key is now based only on name. After settingsFor("tenant-a", "theme", store) caches its value, settingsFor("tenant-b", "theme", store) returns tenant-a's cached setting without calling store.fetch, exposing or applying the wrong tenant's configuration.

findings.title: Preserve the tenant-scoped invalidate API
findings.whyItBreaks: This exported function previously accepted (tenantId, name). Existing TypeScript consumers will fail compilation when passing two arguments; existing JavaScript consumers will silently pass tenantId as name and delete settings:<tenantId> rather than the requested setting entry, leaving stale cached settings.

findings.title: Keep the tenant ID in the settings cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: The key now depends only on name. After tenant A fetches a setting, tenant B requesting the same name receives tenant A's cached value without calling its tenant-specific store.fetch.

findings.title: Keep tenant IDs in cache keys
findings.whyItBreaks: After tenant A reads setting `name`, its value is cached as `settings:name`. A subsequent request by tenant B for the same name hits that entry at line 13 and returns tenant A's value without calling the tenant-scoped store fetch at line 15.

findings.title: Serialize concurrent reservations for the same SKU
findings.whyItBreaks: With stock=1, two calls can both read remaining=1 at line 15, each await save(sku, 0), then each set stock to 0 and return true. The previous synchronous implementation decremented before another caller could observe the same unit, so this PR can over-reserve inventory.

findings.title: Serialize reservations before awaiting persistence
findings.whyItBreaks: Two calls with stock 1 can both read `remaining === 1` before either `await` resumes. Both save 0, both set local stock to 0, and both return true, creating two successful reservations for one unit.

findings.title: Serialize reservations for the same SKU
findings.whyItBreaks: The await yields before stock is updated. Two concurrent reserve("sku") calls with stock 1 both read remaining=1, both persist 0, and both return true, so the application grants two reservations for one unit.

findings.title: Keep retry backoff in milliseconds
findings.whyItBreaks: `retry` still calls `sleep(backoff(a) * 1000)`. At attempt 0, the new value is 1,000, so a retry waits 1,000,000 ms (16m40s) instead of 1s; capped attempts wait 30,000,000 ms (8h20m) instead of 30s.

findings.title: Keep retry delays in milliseconds
findings.whyItBreaks: backoff(0) now returns 1000 milliseconds, but retry() still multiplies it by 1000 before sleep. A first failed attempt therefore waits 1,000,000 ms (16m40s) rather than 1s; subsequent retry delays are likewise 1000× too long.

findings.title: Preserve millisecond units in retry
findings.whyItBreaks: `backoff(0)` now returns 1,000 milliseconds, but `retry` still multiplies it by 1,000 before passing it to its millisecond `sleep` helper. After the first failed attempt, retries wait 1,000,000 ms (about 16.7 minutes) instead of 1,000 ms; later waits are likewise 1,000× too long.

findings.title: Propagate the file close error after flushing
findings.whyItBreaks: The deferred f.Close() return value is ignored. Previously, a successful Flush was followed by `return f.Close()`, so a delayed filesystem error reported at close reached the Save caller. Save is exported, and it now returns nil in that case, causing callers to treat an uncommitted write as successful.

findings.title: Propagate the file close error
findings.whyItBreaks: The deferred f.Close() return value is discarded. Previously, after a successful Flush, Save returned f.Close()'s error; now it returns nil when Flush succeeds even if closing the destination fails. As an exported API, this forces callers to treat that failure as a successful save.

findings.title: Propagate the file close error
findings.whyItBreaks: defer f.Close() ignores its returned error. Previously, after a successful Flush, Save returned f.Close()'s error. Filesystems can report delayed write failures at close, so callers now receive nil and treat a failed save as successful.

findings.title: Include the page’s exclusive end bound
findings.whyItBreaks: _window_bounds defines end as exclusive, but range(start, end - 1) stops one position early. Every page loses its last row; a page containing one row renders empty, and summarize silently omits rows.

findings.title: Include the final row in each page
findings.whyItBreaks: `end` is already exclusive. Using `end - 1` causes `page_window(['a', 'b', 'c'], 0, 2)` to return only `['a']`; a one-row final page returns empty, so `summarize` silently drops rows.

findings.title: Include each page's final row
findings.whyItBreaks: _window_bounds returns a half-open [start, end) range, but this loop stops at end - 1. Every non-empty page loses its final row; with page_size=1, render_page and summarize render no rows at all.

findings.title: Preserve existing keyword-call compatibility
findings.whyItBreaks: All public top-level functions rename their parameters. Existing callers using the base API's keyword arguments (for example, page_window(rows, page=0, size=20)) now receive TypeError for unexpected keyword arguments, despite positional calls continuing to work.

findings.title: Keep entries until their TTL expires
findings.whyItBreaks: Fresh entries have an age below ttlMs, so they are deleted and return null; entries older than ttlMs are returned as valid cache values indefinitely.

findings.title: Remove every completed job without skipping adjacent entries
findings.whyItBreaks: Splicing during forEach shifts the next job into the current index, but forEach advances past it. For `[done, done]`, the second completed job remains in the returned array.

findings.title: Restore the TTL validity comparison
findings.whyItBreaks: A newly stored entry has elapsed time below ttlMs, so this condition is false and get() deletes it and returns null. Once elapsed time exceeds ttlMs, the expired value is returned instead. The cache therefore misses while fresh and serves stale data after expiration.

findings.title: Do not splice while iterating completed jobs
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.splice shifts the next element left while forEach advances its index. For `[doneA, doneB]`, removing doneA at index 0 causes doneB to move to index 0, then forEach advances to index 1 and never examines it; pruneDone returns a still-completed job.

findings.title: Restore cache expiry comparison
findings.whyItBreaks: Fresh entries have age less than ttlMs, so get() deletes them and returns null. Entries older than the TTL are instead returned, allowing stale values to persist.

findings.title: Remove all adjacent completed jobs
findings.whyItBreaks: Splicing during forEach shifts the next job into the current index, but forEach advances to the next index. For `[done, done]`, the second completed job is skipped and returned.

findings.title: Return zero for an empty input
findings.whyItBreaks: With rows=[], reduce returns 0 and rows.length is 0, so this returns NaN instead of the prior numeric empty-set result of 0.

findings.title: Avoid mutating the caller's rows array
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.prototype.sort mutates rows in place. The previous implementation sorted a copy, so callers that reuse their input array now observe it reordered after calling busiest.

findings.title: Preserve the defined empty-input average
findings.whyItBreaks: For an empty array, total is 0 and rows.length is 0, so this now returns NaN. The previous public behavior returned 0, making this an observable compatibility regression for callers that aggregate empty result sets.

findings.title: Do not reorder the caller's rows
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.prototype.sort mutates its receiver. The prior implementation sorted a copy, so callers could reuse `rows` in its original order; this change silently reorders their input while selecting the busiest row.

findings.title: Preserve the empty-input average value
findings.whyItBreaks: `averageAmount([])` now computes `0 / 0`, returning `NaN` instead of the prior numeric default `0`. Consumers of a numeric aggregate can no longer safely use the result for empty datasets.

findings.title: Avoid sorting the caller's array in place
findings.whyItBreaks: `Array.prototype.sort` mutates `rows`. The previous implementation made a defensive copy, so callers that invoke `busiest(rows)` and later rely on the original ordering now observe a reordered array.

findings.title: Sort scores numerically before selecting the cutoff
findings.whyItBreaks: Array#sort() without a comparator compares numbers as strings. With players ordered as [{score: 2}, {score: 10}] and n=1, rankScores returns [2, 10], so cutoff is 2 and topPlayers returns the 2-point player instead of the 10-point player.

findings.title: Sort scores numerically
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.sort() without a comparator compares number values as strings. For players scored [9, 10, 2], reversing produces [9, 2, 10]; with n=1 the cutoff is 9, and the filter/slice returns the first 9-point player instead of the 10-point player.

findings.title: Restore numeric score ordering
findings.whyItBreaks: Default Array.sort compares values as strings. For players ordered as scores 90 then 100 with n=1, the reversed sorted scores are [90, 100], so cutoff is 90 and topPlayers returns the first 90-point player instead of the 100-point player.

findings.title: Use a constant-time comparison for the signature
findings.whyItBreaks: Replacing hmac.compare_digest with normal string equality makes comparison time depend on the matching prefix. A remote attacker can use response timing to progressively forge the HMAC and cause handle() to invoke processor() with an unauthorized payload.

findings.title: Restore constant-time signature comparison
findings.whyItBreaks: Using == can return after the first mismatching character, exposing how much of the attacker-supplied HMAC matches. The distinct 401/200 outcomes at the caller provide an oracle that can enable a remote attacker to recover a valid webhook signature and invoke processor(payload).

findings.title: Use constant-time comparison for webhook signatures
findings.whyItBreaks: Direct string equality can reveal how much of the expected HMAC matches through comparison timing. The changed verification result controls whether an untrusted webhook reaches processor(payload), so an attacker able to make repeated measurements can use the timing oracle to forge an accepted signature.

findings.title: Keep balance updates in the ledger transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: The transaction exits and commits immediately after `_record_ledger`. If either subsequent balance update raises, the ledger records a completed transfer while one or both account balances remain unchanged; if the second update fails, the debit can also persist without the credit. Previously all three writes rolled back together.

findings.title: Keep balance changes in the transfer transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: The ledger insert commits when the `with db.transaction()` block exits. If either subsequent balance update fails, the transfer returns an error after a durable ledger entry already records it; if the second update fails after the debit, balances can also be left asymmetric. Previously all three writes rolled back together.

findings.title: Keep ledger and balance changes in one transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: The transaction at lines 22-23 completes before either balance update runs. If either update fails, the ledger insert can no longer be rolled back; if the destination update fails after the source update, the debit can also be left without its matching credit. Before this change all three writes were in the same transaction.

findings.title: Keep billing-day boundaries in UTC
findings.whyItBreaks: The previous implementation consistently derived the billing date in UTC. The new local getters make the result depend on the server's timezone: for example, at 2026-01-01T00:30:00Z, a server in America/Los_Angeles returns 2025-12-31 instead of 2026-01-01. This can split or merge billing-day comparisons differently across deployments.

findings.title: Keep billing-day keys in UTC
findings.whyItBreaks: This replaces the prior UTC contract with the runtime host's local timezone. Under TZ=America/Los_Angeles, `billingDay(new Date('2026-01-01T00:30:00Z'))` now returns `2025-12-31` instead of `2026-01-01`; `sameBillingDay` can therefore split two instants that belong to the same prior UTC billing date.

findings.title: Keep billing dates in UTC
findings.whyItBreaks: This changes the established UTC contract to the machine's local timezone. For example, 2026-01-01T00:30:00Z now becomes 2025-12-31 on a Los Angeles host, changing billing-day keys and sameBillingDay classification based on deployment timezone.

findings.title: Include tenant in the memoization key
findings.whyItBreaks: After tenant A caches account X, a read for tenant B and account X returns tenant A's Profile from memo and skips fetchProfile. This returns the wrong tenant's profile whenever account identifiers overlap.

findings.title: Keep tenant in the profile cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: After reading account `a` for tenant `t1`, a request for account `a` in tenant `t2` returns the cached `t1` Profile and never calls its fetcher. This can display or expose one tenant's profile to another.

findings.title: Restore tenant scoping in the profile cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: After readProfile("tenant-a", "acct", ...) caches tenant-a's profile, readProfile("tenant-b", "acct", ...) returns that cached profile at line 16 without calling fetchProfile. This exposes incorrect tenant data across the tenancy boundary.

findings.title: Propagate missing-key failures
findings.whyItBreaks: A missing key previously threw Error(`missing: ${key}`), but now returns "", which is a valid store value. Callers cannot distinguish absent data from an explicitly stored empty string; loadAll consequently returns partial data instead of failing when any requested key is absent.

findings.title: Preserve missing-key failures from load
findings.whyItBreaks: A missing key now becomes an indistinguishable empty string. `loadAll` maps that fallback into its returned array, whereas it previously propagated the missing-key error, so callers can treat absent data as a legitimately stored empty value.

findings.title: Preserve the missing-key error
findings.whyItBreaks: A missing key previously threw `Error("missing: <key>")`; the new catch converts it to `""`, which is indistinguishable from a legitimately stored empty string. `loadAll` now returns partial-looking data instead of failing when any requested key is absent.

findings.title: Retain compatibility with timeoutMs configurations
findings.whyItBreaks: Existing TypeScript callers using the exported Config shape with { maxAttempts, timeoutMs } no longer type-check because timeout and retries are newly required. Untyped callers instead read config.timeout as undefined: Date.now() + undefined is NaN, so the deadline guard is always false and retry ignores the previously configured timeout.

findings.title: Keep the existing Config fields compatible
findings.whyItBreaks: Existing consumers provide `timeoutMs`; `retry` now reads the absent `timeout`, making `Date.now() + undefined` evaluate to `NaN`. The deadline guard at line 10 never rejects `NaN`, so JavaScript consumers ignore their timeout, while TypeScript consumers also fail because both `timeout` and the unrelated required `retries` field are missing.

findings.title: Expose exhaustion failures from retryBackground
findings.whyItBreaks: Every exception from `fn` is discarded. After retries are exhausted or the deadline is reached, the exported function returns `void`, indistinguishable from its successful `return` at line 26, so callers cannot detect that no attempt succeeded.

findings.title: Run the initial attempt before consuming retries
findings.whyItBreaks: `retries` is used as the total invocation count. Consequently, `retries: 0` never calls `fn`, and `retries: N` makes only N attempts rather than one initial attempt plus N retries.

findings.title: Keep the existing retry Config fields compatible
findings.whyItBreaks: Existing TypeScript callers of retry using { maxAttempts, timeoutMs } no longer type-check; they must also provide the irrelevant new retries field. Existing JavaScript callers still compile but config.timeout is undefined, so Date.now() + undefined becomes NaN and the timeout guard never stops retries.

findings.title: Run retryBackground off the caller's execution path
findings.whyItBreaks: retryBackground promises background execution, but it immediately invokes fn and synchronously loops until success, timeout, or exhaustion. A caller using this exported API will block for the full retry work instead of returning while it runs in the background.

findings.title: Preserve failures from retryBackground
findings.whyItBreaks: Every exception from fn is discarded, and exhaustion or timeout returns normally just like a successful callback. This new exported API forces callers to treat a failed background operation as success.

findings.title: Handle numeric Field values before reading length
findings.whyItBreaks: `FieldProps.value` now accepts `number`, but numbers have no `length`. Type-checking rejects this access; if emitted without type-checking, `<Field value={42} />` renders `len=undefined` instead of a meaningful label.

findings.title: Handle numeric values before reading their length
findings.whyItBreaks: FieldProps now publicly accepts number values (line 2), but numbers have no length property. <Field value={42} /> produces "len=undefined" at runtime; TypeScript type checking also rejects value.length on string | number.

findings.title: Handle numeric values before reading .length
findings.whyItBreaks: FieldProps now publicly accepts number, but number has no length. TypeScript reports an invalid property access, and an unchecked runtime call such as <Field value={42}> renders "len=undefined" rather than a valid length.

findings.title: Restore the Git output buffer limit
findings.whyItBreaks: The adapter uses this helper to collect the full `git diff` output. Without `maxBuffer`, `spawnSync` applies Node's 1 MiB default; a larger PR causes `git diff` to terminate with `ERR_CHILD_PROCESS_STDIO_MAXBUFFER`, and `runGithub` reports the review as failed instead of reviewing the PR.

findings.title: Restore the Git diff buffer limit
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing maxBuffer changes spawnSync's stdout limit from 64 MiB to Node's 1 MiB default. The patch is collected through this helper at line 140, so a PR whose diff exceeds 1 MiB causes git diff to fail before any review is produced.

findings.title: Preserve a sufficient buffer for PR diffs
findings.whyItBreaks: Without maxBuffer, spawnSync uses its 1 MiB default. The unpaged `git diff` at line 140 can exceed that on a normal large PR; spawnSync then returns a non-zero/null status and this helper throws, so the review check fails instead of reviewing the PR.

findings.title: Restore the enforced read-only sandbox
findings.whyItBreaks: runCodex supplies an arbitrary prompt to Codex with cwd set to opts.repoPath. Without the explicit -s read-only, a loaded Codex configuration can select workspace-write or danger-full-access, allowing the agent to modify the reviewed repository during a run that is expected to return review text. The previous argument forced the non-mutating boundary.

findings.title: Force Codex to run read-only
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing `-s read-only` makes `codex exec` use its configured sandbox. In environments configured for `workspace-write`, the agent can edit the target repository because this function runs it with `cwd: opts.repoPath`; a review invocation can therefore alter the code it is meant only to inspect.

findings.title: Keep the Codex child in read-only mode
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing `-s read-only` makes the effective sandbox depend on Codex configuration. A writable configured sandbox lets the prompt-driven child modify or delete files under `opts.repoPath`, whereas this review runner previously prevented such writes.

findings.title: Diff against the PR head from its merge base
findings.whyItBreaks: PR_BASE_SHA may be a newer base-branch tip than the PR's fork point, while PR_HEAD_SHA identifies the commit being reviewed. Diffing baseSha directly to HEAD then includes base-only changes as apparent deletions. It also ignores PR_HEAD_SHA when the checkout is a PR merge ref, although line 178 posts the review against headSha. The resulting bundle can review changes absent from the PR head and produce inline comments that GitHub cannot attach to that commit.

findings.title: Diff against the PR head's merge base
findings.whyItBreaks: When PR_BASE_SHA is the current target-branch tip and that branch advanced after the PR forked, `git diff baseSha HEAD` includes target-branch-only changes as deletions/additions. It also ignores PR_HEAD_SHA even though the resulting review is posted to `headSha` at line 178. The reviewer can therefore analyze or comment on changes that are not in the reviewed PR commit.

findings.title: Compute the PR diff from the merge base
findings.whyItBreaks: PR_BASE_SHA may be a newer base-branch commit than the feature branch's fork point. `git diff baseSha HEAD` then includes reverse changes from that newer base commit back to the actual merge base, so the review bundle and inline-comment path set contain files not changed by the PR.

findings.title: Use the selected PR head for the review diff
findings.whyItBreaks: When PR_HEAD_SHA overrides the local checkout (for example, a checkout of a synthetic merge commit), the bundle and posted review target `headSha`, but `patch` and `changedFiles` are derived from local `HEAD`. The reviewer can therefore analyze merge-checkout content while publishing findings against a different PR commit.

findings.title: Preserve literal prompt content during placeholder interpolation
findings.whyItBreaks: String.prototype.replace interprets `$&`, `$'`, `$`` and `$$` in a string replacement. A reviewed patch containing `$&`, for example, is inserted into the critic prompt as `{{PATCH}}` rather than its literal source text; the same corruption can affect the bundle and candidate JSON. runCodex then reviews a malformed prompt.

findings.title: Preserve literal prompt data
findings.whyItBreaks: String replacement text interprets $&, $`, $', and $$ specially. A patch containing "$&" is inserted into the critic prompt as "{{PATCH}}" rather than the literal source text; other tokens can duplicate surrounding prompt content. The previous callback replacements inserted all bundle, finding, and patch data verbatim.

findings.title: Preserve literal prompt payloads
findings.whyItBreaks: String replacement values interpret `$&`, `$`` and `$'` specially. A patch or serialized bundle containing `$&` now inserts the placeholder text (for example, `{{PATCH}}`) instead of the literal source content; other tokens can duplicate prompt prefixes/suffixes. This corrupts the prompts sent to both review stages.

findings.title: Keep fallback reviews pinned to the analyzed SHA
findings.whyItBreaks: When the initial request fails (for example, because an inline comment is rejected) and the PR receives a new commit before the fallback runs, the fallback omits commit_id. GitHub then defaults the review to the PR's most recent commit, while this run's result was computed from headSha. That can post stale findings or REQUEST_CHANGES against a commit the review never analyzed.

findings.title: Keep the analyzed commit on the fallback review
findings.whyItBreaks: When the inline-comment POST fails, this fallback now omits commit_id. GitHub then defaults the review to the PR's most recent commit, while this run analyzed the earlier headSha captured at src/adapters/github.ts:141-144. If a new commit is pushed during review processing, a REQUEST_CHANGES or COMMENT result for the old diff is published against the newer, unreviewed commit.

findings.title: Pin fallback reviews to the reviewed commit
findings.whyItBreaks: When the primary request fails (for example, due to an invalid inline comment), this retry no longer sends the SHA used to build the review. GitHub defaults an omitted commit_id to the PR's most recent commit, so a push received while review() is running makes an old result appear as a review of the new commit.

findings.title: Reject malformed findings instead of fabricating defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: A valid Partial<Finding> such as {} now becomes a reported P1/bug finding with an empty file and line 0. Previously this malformed input raised an error (or was omitted by normalizeReview(..., false)), so callers could distinguish invalid model output from a real finding.

findings.title: Reject malformed required finding fields
findings.whyItBreaks: Invalid review data that previously raised an error is now returned as a seemingly valid finding. For example, an unknown severity becomes P1 and missing file/line fields become "" and 0, so callers cannot distinguish malformed model output from a real P1 issue.

findings.title: Reject malformed findings instead of fabricating defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: Invalid severity/category and required-field failures that previously threw now become P1/bug findings with empty locations and explanations. normalizeReview therefore returns a seemingly valid review for malformed input, and its caller cannot distinguish that failure from a real finding.

findings.title: Restore explicit repository selection for manual runs
findings.whyItBreaks: On workflow_dispatch, EVENT_HEAD is empty and this runs before actions/checkout. With neither -R, GH_REPO, nor a checked-out git remote available, `gh pr view "$PR_NUM"` cannot identify the target repository. Its nonzero exit is hidden by the surrounding echo command substitution, so empty head/base outputs reach the checkout step instead of the requested PR SHAs.

findings.title: Keep an explicit repository when resolving manual PR refs
findings.whyItBreaks: For workflow_dispatch, EVENT_HEAD is empty, so this pre-checkout branch runs. gh pr view now has neither -R nor GH_REPO, and there is no repository checkout until line 43 from which gh can infer one. On a clean self-hosted runner, resolving the PR therefore fails and the requested manual review never reaches checkout.

findings.title: Keep the repository target for manually dispatched PR resolution
findings.whyItBreaks: On workflow_dispatch, EVENT_HEAD is empty, so this branch runs before actions/checkout. Without -R "$REPO", gh pr view must infer a repository from the runner working directory; an uninitialized workspace fails resolution, while a retained self-hosted workspace can resolve the same PR number from the wrong repository. The checkout then receives missing or incorrect SHA outputs.

findings.title: Preserve malformed-review errors instead of returning an empty review
findings.whyItBreaks: Inputs such as {}, null, or a response missing findings/checked/residual_risks previously threw a malformed-review error. They now normalize to an empty summary with no findings and no blocking residual risks, making malformed agent output indistinguishable from a successful clean review. As an exported function, this forces every caller to conflate failure with a legitimate result.

findings.title: Reject malformed required review fields
findings.whyItBreaks: Inputs that previously raised a malformed-output error, such as null or an object with findings: {}, now produce a RawReview with empty arrays and an empty summary. This exported API makes producer failure indistinguishable from a legitimate review with no findings.

findings.title: Reject malformed review output
findings.whyItBreaks: Inputs such as null or an object missing required fields now return a successful RawReview with an empty summary and arrays. This conflates a malformed reviewer response with a legitimate no-findings review; before this change the malformed-output error reached the caller.

findings.title: Restore PR ref resolution for manual reviews
findings.whyItBreaks: A workflow_dispatch event has no pull_request payload. These expressions therefore check out github.ref (the workflow branch selected by the operator), default the base branch to main, and pass empty PR_BASE_SHA/PR_HEAD_SHA values. Running the required pr_number for a PR on another branch can consequently execute an unrelated revision instead of the PR's own reviewer code and lacks its explicit comparison refs.

findings.title: Resolve the requested PR before manual-dispatch checkout
findings.whyItBreaks: workflow_dispatch has no pull_request payload, so github.event.pull_request.head.sha is empty and this expression falls back to github.ref—the branch/tag selected to run the workflow, not the input pr_number's head. A manual run can therefore execute Needlefish from main or another selected ref instead of the requested PR's revision; the same event also leaves PR_BASE_SHA and PR_HEAD_SHA empty at lines 45-46.

findings.title: Restore requested-PR ref resolution for manual dispatches
findings.whyItBreaks: A workflow_dispatch event supplies pr_number but has no pull_request payload. These expressions therefore fall back to github.ref for checkout, fetch main, and pass empty PR_BASE_SHA/PR_HEAD_SHA to the reviewer. Manual runs can consequently execute the selected workflow branch rather than the requested PR head and lack that PR's base/head pair; the removed step previously queried those exact refs with gh pr view.

findings.title: Restore a buffer large enough for review diffs
findings.whyItBreaks: runLocal passes the complete output of `git diff baseSha HEAD` through this helper at line 100. Without `maxBuffer`, spawnSync uses its 1 MiB default; a larger diff terminates the child with a max-buffer error, and line 12 then throws instead of producing a review. The prior 64 MiB limit supported these inputs.

findings.title: Restore the 64 MiB diff buffer
findings.whyItBreaks: Without maxBuffer, spawnSync uses its 1 MiB default and terminates git when stdout exceeds it. runLocal obtains the complete review input via `git(["diff", baseSha, "HEAD"], cwd)` at line 100, so any valid 1–64 MiB PR now throws at line 12 instead of being reviewed.

findings.title: Restore the buffer limit for patch generation
findings.whyItBreaks: `runLocal` collects the complete `git diff` at line 100. Without `maxBuffer`, Node's `spawnSync` default is 1 MiB; a larger diff terminates git and `git()` throws, so the local review cannot run. The previous 64 MiB limit supported these valid review inputs.

findings.title: Keep failed reviews in a failing check state
findings.whyItBreaks: When review() throws, this posts the completed Needlefish check as neutral even though the error path says the PR did not pass. GitHub treats neutral as a successful required-check status, so a protected branch requiring Needlefish can permit merging an unreviewed PR.

findings.title: Select the target repository for PR diff retrieval
findings.whyItBreaks: gh pr diff resolves its repository from the process working directory unless --repo is supplied, but runGithub's target repository is provided separately through GITHUB_REPOSITORY and cwd. Invoking the adapter from another directory can therefore fail to fetch a diff or fetch the same PR number from the wrong repository.

findings.title: Bind `gh pr diff` to `GITHUB_REPOSITORY`
findings.whyItBreaks: `ghText` inherits the process working directory and this command has no `--repo`, unlike the other GitHub API calls. When the supplied `cwd` differs from the process directory (or that directory is not the target repository), `gh pr diff` resolves a different repository or fails, while the resulting review is posted to `GITHUB_REPOSITORY`.

findings.title: Keep review execution failures blocking
findings.whyItBreaks: The catch path is reached when the review or its publication fails, but now publishes a `neutral` Needlefish check. GitHub treats `neutral` as a successful required status, so a repository requiring this check can merge a PR that Needlefish did not review successfully.

findings.title: Keep review failures blocking
findings.whyItBreaks: GitHub treats a completed neutral check as successful for required-status-check protection. When review(), postReview(), or the successful postCheck() path throws, this catch path now publishes Needlefish as neutral even though its summary says the review did not pass; a PR requiring Needlefish can therefore merge without a completed review.

findings.title: Restore the trusted Needlefish checkout
findings.whyItBreaks: The head commit contains only .github/workflows/review.yml and .needlefish/answers.json; it has neither package.json nor src/cli.ts. Consequently pnpm install has no project manifest and the subsequent tsx src/cli.ts invocation cannot start the reviewer, so every review job fails instead of reviewing the PR.

findings.title: Do not execute the PR checkout as the reviewer
findings.whyItBreaks: The workflow checks out the PR head, then installs and executes its dependency graph and src/cli.ts while GH_TOKEN is available with pull-requests: write and checks: write permissions. Once this workflow is merged, a same-repository PR can add a manifest/lockfile and reviewer source that suppresses or forges the review result, defeating the review gate.

The PR-controlled reviewer can write pull-request reviews or checks.
The workflow executes Needlefish's reviewer implementation from the untrusted PR-head checkout.
The PR-controlled reviewer can write pull-request reviews or checks.

findings.title: Restore the trusted checkout for the review tool
findings.whyItBreaks: The command executes src/cli.ts from the PR-head checkout. An internal PR can modify that file (or package install hooks) to suppress findings or forge review output; the job supplies a token with pull-requests: write and checks: write. The removed separate main checkout was the boundary preventing the reviewed code from controlling its reviewer.

findings.title: Run installation from a checkout that contains the tool
findings.whyItBreaks: The PR-head repository contains only .github/workflows/review.yml and .needlefish/answers.json; it has no package.json, pnpm-lock.yaml, or src/cli.ts. Running pnpm install in that checkout therefore cannot install the tool, and the subsequent CLI path is absent, so every review job fails before producing a review.

facts.meaning: The workflow executes Needlefish's reviewer implementation from the untrusted PR-head checkout.
The PR-controlled reviewer can write pull-request reviews or checks.
The workflow executes Needlefish's reviewer implementation from the untrusted PR-head checkout.
The PR-controlled reviewer can write pull-request reviews or checks.

findings.title: Restore a checkout containing the reviewer package
findings.whyItBreaks: The checked-out repository at head contains only .github/workflows/review.yml and .needlefish/answers.json; it has no package.json, lockfile, node_modules, or src/cli.ts. Installing at the workspace root and then invoking ./node_modules/.bin/tsx src/cli.ts therefore cannot run the reviewer.

findings.title: Run the reviewer from a trusted checkout
findings.whyItBreaks: This command executes src/cli.ts from the PR head checked out at lines 43-47, with GH_TOKEN granted pull-requests:write and checks:write and on a self-hosted runner. A same-repository PR can add or alter the CLI (and its install inputs) to execute arbitrary code, exfiltrate the token, forge review/check output, or compromise the runner. The removed second checkout previously kept the executable reviewer pinned to frankekn/needlefish@main.

facts.meaning: The workflow executes Needlefish's reviewer implementation from the untrusted PR-head checkout.
The PR-controlled reviewer can write pull-request reviews or checks.
The workflow executes Needlefish's reviewer implementation from the untrusted PR-head checkout.
The PR-controlled reviewer can write pull-request reviews or checks.

findings.title: Preserve case-insensitive severity normalization
findings.whyItBreaks: Review output is parsed from untyped input by normalizeReview. A finding with severity " p0 " or "p0", which the previous normalizer correctly emitted as P0, now fails the exact-match check and is silently emitted as P3. This downgrades the reported severity of a real finding.

findings.title: Keep invalid severities conservatively classified
findings.whyItBreaks: The prior normalization accepted common raw values such as " p0 " or "p2" by trimming and uppercasing them. The new exact-membership check rejects those values and returns P3, so a critical or normal finding is silently reported as low severity. It also changes the fallback for absent/unrecognized severities from P1 to P3, further understating malformed review output.

findings.title: Preserve canonicalization before validating severity
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeReview accepts untyped external JSON, but this now tests raw.severity verbatim. A finding with severity "p0" or " P2 " previously normalized to P0/P2; it now fails the whitelist and is emitted as P3, potentially downgrading a blocking finding.

findings.title: Keep GitHub tokens out of the Codex child
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing the explicit environment copy and redaction makes spawnSync inherit GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN, and GITHUB_API_TOKEN. The invoked Codex process receives caller-supplied prompts and examines opts.repoPath, so untrusted repository content or prompt injection can cause CI GitHub credentials to be disclosed or used.

findings.title: Keep GitHub tokens out of the Codex subprocess
findings.whyItBreaks: Without an explicit env object, spawnSync inherits process.env. This passes GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN, and GITHUB_API_TOKEN into the Codex process; a repository instruction or prompt injection can read a token and return it in the model output despite the read-only filesystem sandbox. The prior implementation explicitly removed these credentials.

findings.title: Keep GitHub tokens out of the Codex subprocess
findings.whyItBreaks: Without an explicit env object, spawnSync inherits process.env. This passes GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN, and GITHUB_API_TOKEN to Codex while it processes the supplied prompt and repository; a malicious instruction or tool invocation can use or exfiltrate credentials that the previous code deliberately withheld.

findings.title: Restore the same-repository guard
findings.whyItBreaks: Fork-origin pull requests can now start this self-hosted job. The workflow checks out the fork head SHA (line 23) and directly executes its src/cli.ts (line 34), allowing an attacker to run arbitrary code on the runner and access its filesystem, persistent state, and any runner-available credentials.

findings.title: Restore the same-repository guard for the self-hosted job
findings.whyItBreaks: Fork PRs now dispatch this self-hosted job, which checks out the fork-controlled head SHA and executes its src/cli.ts. An attacker can submit a fork PR that runs arbitrary commands in the runner environment, compromising any persistent runner credentials, workspace state, or network access.

findings.title: Restore the same-repository guard before running PR code
findings.whyItBreaks: The removed job-level condition previously skipped fork PRs. Fork pull_request events now check out the attacker-controlled head SHA and execute its dependency installation and src/cli.ts on a self-hosted runner. A fork author can modify the reviewed code to execute arbitrary commands on that runner.

findings.title: Keep zero-duration runner settings valid
findings.whyItBreaks: Existing deployments using either timeout environment variable as "0" to request immediate escalation now silently receive the 5000 ms or 2000 ms fallback. This changes a previously accepted configuration and can delay timeout completion by seven seconds.

findings.title: Preserve zero-duration environment overrides
findings.whyItBreaks: With either runner-duration environment variable set to "0", the previous predicate returned 0; this change instead returns the fallback. Consequently NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0 now waits 5000 ms before SIGKILL (line 124), and NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=0 now waits 2000 ms before resolving the timed-out invocation (line 123), breaking an existing no-additional-delay configuration on upgrade.

findings.title: Keep zero-valued runner delay overrides valid
findings.whyItBreaks: Existing deployments using NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0 now receive the 5000 ms fallback, delaying SIGKILL by five seconds after a timeout. Likewise, NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=0 now waits the 2000 ms fallback before resolving. The base implementation explicitly accepted zero, so this is an upgrade regression for valid configured behavior.

findings.title: Deep-review every changed file
findings.whyItBreaks: Large reviews select only six hotspots. Removing the tail-coverage hotspot leaves files omitted by the mapper, or assigned to lower-ranked hotspots, with no deep review at all; the final critic receives only the patch stat and can return a clean verdict despite unreviewed changes.

findings.title: Convert failed deep passes to blocking results
findings.whyItBreaks: If one deep Codex response is malformed or its invocation fails, normalizeReview/extractJson now throws out of reviewLarge. The prior behavior continued the remaining reviews and returned a blocking residual risk, whereas callers now receive no structured review verdict.

findings.title: Forward residual risks from deep reviews
findings.whyItBreaks: A successful deep review can report blocks=true when evidence is insufficient, but the merged candidate now always supplies residual_risks: []. The critic cannot distinguish that failure-to-verify signal from a clean review, so the final verdict can pass an incompletely reviewed large change.

findings.title: Resolve critic revision placeholders
findings.whyItBreaks: The unchanged critic template previously received baseSha and headSha. Removing both substitutions leaves its revision placeholders unresolved; in the large-review path the critic has only a patch stat, so it cannot inspect the actual base..head diff when validating or pruning findings.

findings.title: Keep the failure reason in finding deduplication
findings.whyItBreaks: Distinct findings at the same location and category now collide whenever their normalized titles share the first 60 characters, regardless of different failure reasons. One is silently removed before the critic sees it; the previous key kept an 80-character reason prefix specifically to avoid that loss.

findings.title: Preserve blocking residual risks from deep reviews
findings.whyItBreaks: A deep review can return a blocking residual risk when it cannot safely conclude PASS, but this code now constructs candidateMerged with residual_risks: []. The critic and deriveVerdict therefore cannot distinguish that blocked result from a clean review, so a large PR with no findings can be approved despite a deep pass explicitly requiring a block.

findings.title: Restore deep review coverage for unmapped changed files
findings.whyItBreaks: Large reviews retain only the first six mapped hotspots. The deleted tail-coverage path was the only mechanism that added changed files omitted by those selected hotspots. When the mapper returns a selected set that does not cover every changed file, those files receive no deep review; the critic receives only patchStat, not their diff.

findings.title: Keep partial large reviews structured after a deep-pass failure
findings.whyItBreaks: runCodex, extractJson, and normalizeReview can throw for one malformed or failed deep pass. Previously that failure was converted into a blocking residual risk and the remaining hotspots were reviewed. It now rejects review() outright, so a transient failure in any one hotspot prevents callers from receiving the structured blocked review result.

findings.title: Deep-review files excluded by the hotspot cap
findings.whyItBreaks: The first six hotspots are now the complete review set. A mapper result with more than six hotspots, or one that omits a changed file, leaves those files out of the loop at line 97 with no tail review or blocking residual risk, so a large PR can receive a verdict without its changed file being deep-reviewed.

findings.title: Forward deep-pass residual risks to the final verdict
findings.whyItBreaks: A deep reviewer can return a blocking residual risk when it cannot safely conclude a review. This code now replaces all such signals with an empty array before the critic runs, allowing the critic and deriveVerdict to treat an unresolved large review as clear.

findings.title: Retain partial results when a hotspot pass fails
findings.whyItBreaks: A malformed or failed deep Codex response now throws out of reviewLarge immediately. Previously, the failure was recorded as a blocking residual risk and the other hotspots could still be returned, so one transient hotspot failure now makes the entire large-review workflow fail without a review result.

findings.title: Keep the failure reason in the deduplication key
findings.whyItBreaks: Distinct findings on the same changed line and category now collide whenever their normalized title prefixes match in the first 60 characters, even if their whyItBreaks fields identify separate defects. The map retains only the higher-severity one and silently drops the other; the prior key deliberately distinguished the reason text.

findings.title: Restore focus interpolation for large reviews
findings.whyItBreaks: The deep-pass prompt no longer replaces {{FOCUS}} with bundle.focus. For patches routed through reviewLarge, a caller-provided focus directive is therefore not passed to any hotspot review (and may remain as a literal placeholder), unlike the previous behavior.

findings.title: Preserve focus in the large-review prompts
findings.whyItBreaks: Large patches now construct the map prompt without bundle.focus, and the per-hotspot prompt no longer substitutes {{FOCUS}}. A caller-specified focus therefore affects small reviews but is ignored for large reviews, causing the requested review area to be deprioritized or missed.

findings.title: Preserve focus when building large-review prompts
findings.whyItBreaks: The large-review path previously supplied bundle.focus to both the map pass and each hotspot deep pass. After this change, a caller’s requested review focus is absent from every prompt whenever isLarge(bundle) selects this path, so targeted large reviews are performed as unfocused reviews.

findings.title: Carry rounded seconds into minutes
findings.whyItBreaks: For durations from 119500ms through 119999ms, minutes is calculated as 1 before the remaining 59.5+ seconds round to 60, so rendered review stats display `1m 60s` instead of the correctly rounded `2m 0s`.

findings.title: Normalize rounded seconds before rendering
findings.whyItBreaks: For a 119500 ms duration, this computes minutes=1 and seconds=60, rendering `1m 60s` instead of the rounded duration `2m 0s`. Both per-call stats and total duration use this formatter.

findings.title: Carry rounded seconds into minutes
findings.whyItBreaks: For a duration such as 119500 ms, `minutes` is computed as 1 before the 59500 ms remainder rounds to 60 seconds, so rendered review stats show `1m 60s` instead of `2m 0s`.

findings.title: Reject zero in parsePositiveInteger
findings.whyItBreaks: For input "0", both conditions are false, so this exported function returns 0 even though its name and error contract promise a positive integer.

findings.title: Reject zero to preserve the positive-integer contract
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed guard accepts "0" and returns 0, while the exported function name and its error contract promise a positive integer. Consumers relying on this public parser can now receive zero where a strictly positive value is required.

findings.title: Reject zero in parsePositiveInteger
findings.whyItBreaks: Changing the guard to `parsed < 0` makes `parsePositiveInteger("0", label)` return 0, despite both its exported name and error contract requiring a positive integer. Public callers can therefore accept zero as a validated positive value.
